If all of this is correct:

The most important questions to ask are: where is the MPL and has price already consumed the FOF at this level? If so, move down to the next MPL and ask the same question. Keep dropping down in scale until you find a MPL that still has FOF.

Tricks are fakeouts. Two important concepts to know about every FO:

1. Did the FO take the extreme set of orders of the FL its a reaction to? 2. Where was the DP to FO?

** The decision point to FO is important because it is the future engulf of this DP that leads to the FTR that contains FOF and the next origin of a move up/down. There is also an MPL associated with this FTR.

This also might explain why sometimes price FO to the DP above an obvious supply level...the MPL of the DP wasn't hit yet.

Something I have been noticing...I wonder if anyone else sees this too:

First, I think there is a difference between "true supply/demand (FOF) (origin up/down)" and the extreme end of a FTR that forms the edge of a FL Box. The True supply/demand doesn't always form in the FTR.

We draw Fl Boxes based on the break of swap levels, therefore we draw FL boxes based on the break of FTR's.

Example:

This becomes important when we look to ID an engulf....are we looking for an engulf of a FL Box or an engulf of the "true supply/demand/FOF/Origin up down" within the FL Box?

Both seem important...

So I started looking at areas of historical charts and I noticed some of the best reactions came from areas where there was an engulf of both the origin of a move up/down (FOF) and the top/bottom of its associated FL Box. Why is this especially important?

1. The engulf of a FL Box indicates an engulf of a swap zone (and the potential forming of a new opposing one) 2. An engulf of Origin up/down (FOF) indicates consumption of all opposing order flow, and newly executed FOF exists as a result.

We can draw lots of FL Boxes, but not every FL Box holds an important origin up/down. When an important FL Box (with an origin up/down located within it) is engulfed, the new zone formed is highly likely to react when price returns.

I've noticed an EG of the origin (FOF) is followed by a FTR, but it often turns into a confirmed FL once price continues on to break the extreme of the FL Box as well, and comes back to test the FTR. This ends up looking like a DP located just under a newly formed FL Box. The big bounce happens later on, when price returns to this area, and forms a FO to the 'DP' below the new FL Box (the DP is just the FL formed after engulfing the opposing origin. While the new FL Box is important to establish a new swap zone formation, the new FOF that is formed after the engulf of the opposing origin is where all the new orders exist. When they combine, the result is a very strong level with potential to bounce price quite far. (or at least this is what i have noticed recently, as always I could be wrong ).

Here is a drawing: This is how I normally draw FL Boxes

Next I will post a real life chart example:

USD-CAD:

Here, FL Box B is formed when price engulf the True Supply located within FL Box A. Then, price RT a little bit before engulfing the extreme high of FL Box A (making FL Box C).

We are left with two closely related FL Boxes...one created a new swap level by engulfing the opposing one (this is FL Box C) and the other engulfed opposing True Supply and is the location for newly executed FOF (Buy orders). Even though FL Box B looks like a DP below FL Box C, it is very important as the area of true FOF.

When price returns later on, it bounces very strongly off the newly formed FOF - as you can see, FL Box B and FL Box C work together (like a 'special' combined FL Box) to create extra strength. This is also a ORFL...

And..here is a simplified version showing the special combined FL Box/ORFL & the reaction that happened when price returns to it.

Very low risk...incredibly high return.
